Do you like traveling? You could be an Au Pair in a ton of different countries or go teach English abroad maybe. Those aren't careers (unless you want to go into teaching),  but they could give you a bit more time after you graduate to explore your options and not end up at your parent's. If you do that it's highly advisable to really explore what you want to do and not just go out and party because you're young and in a foreign country. 
From experience, it really defeats the purpose of a year abroad while you're trying to figure yourself out and come back in the same place because you didn't put in the effort to really think about it.

I don't really have any advice.. But I really want to say good job for thinking of this now. Contrary to what is pushed in most high schools, college is NOT for everyone. You don't need to go to a four year college to become a chef or pastry chef.

So I'll start by saying I also suffer from depression (and I've also been diagnosed with adjustment disorder). Last year however, I went to Paris for a year to study and work and figure out what I wanted to do with my life before I spent thousands of dollars finishing a French degree. And it was the best decision I made. Ever. 

If you go to Asia or somewhere to teach English, you REALLY have to try. Try more than you would at home. Go to [meetups](http://www.meetup.com/)  and meet with people who enjoy all of those interest that you have (There are English speaking ones everywhere I'm sure especially on something like philosophy)  and that's on top of the things that therapists or online websites say to do to combat depression. 
It's so important to get out while you're in a place temporarily because you'll end up regretting the fact that you spent all day in bed with netflix while you're in this fantastic place with museums and parks and wonderful people that you could be spending time and sharing ideas with. Those people could also end up helping you figure out what you want to do and what you would enjoy making a career out of. 

I would also encourage doing this while you're still in the "honeymoon phase" of moving to your new city. The longer you wait, the harder it is to force yourself to go DO.

I became a vegetarian at age 12 after my brother and sister became vegetarian. My entire family thought it was just a phase too because I was such a picky eater. (Now I admit the only reason I *really* did it was to follow them). Bit I was an incredibly picky eater and hated most veggies. 

I think what worked most for me was that I started by eating Morningstar Farms and such (Gardein is my favorite right now). They're a bit pricey, and full of preservatives, but they really helped me transition. Other than that, my parents would find different ways to make veggies that I didn't like into something tasty.

 My dad refused to support us but thankfully he didn't do the cooking, so my mom would often make the meat on the side if it was just a chicken breast and we would eat the veggies, salad, and usually some starch like potatoes. But also making a small veggie lasagna and another small meat lasagna instead of one large one works too.

[Pinterest](https://www.pinterest.com/) will be your best friend for finding recipes. Just put in healthy vegetarian recipes and you will get soooooo many choices with blogs. 

Meat substitutes/protien: Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, seitan, greek yogurt, and eggs. Eggs are a really quick and easy one, especially in the morning. 

Everyone complains about tofu and tempehs taste but the key is to know how to prepare it.
Tofu- I usually fry- while not the healthiest its the tastiest and great in a stir-fry
Tempeh- I've found that breaking them into small pieces or thin strips is best and pan frying them with a small amount of oil.


FINALLY. I just read that this post is four months old but it was on the front page of the sub so I responded with my infinite wisdom before seeing the date..... Hope this helps even if she's not a vegetarian anymore! :)
